1:
The chapter opens with a register, and the witnesses read its heading — “these are now the chief of their fathers, and this is the genealogy of them that went up with me from Babylon” — as the muster-roll of a second exodus. The reformed John Gill takes the words plainly as the caption of the list that runs on to the close of the section, naming the chief of the fathers whose descent is then traced house by house. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains the form of the register: the names of the heads of houses are followed generally by that of the wider families to which they belonged, and the whole is to be compared with the roll of those who had gone up with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:2 and following, the earlier return whose pattern this later one repeats.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the bare heading into the drama of a fresh migration. Ezra, having received his commission from the king, beats up for volunteers, as it were, setting up an ensign to assemble the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah in the very language of Isaiah 11:12. One would think, Henry marvels, that under such a leader and with such encouragements all the Jews would at length have shaken themselves from their dust; yet multitudes stayed behind, loving their ease better than their religion, believing not that Jerusalem would better their condition. But some offered themselves willingly, and the heads of the several families are named here for their honour, the numbers of the males each brought in amounting in all to 1496. Two priests are named and one of the sons of David, though these seem to have come without their families, intending to see how they liked Jerusalem before sending for them.

Henry notices too that several of the clans named here — Parosh, Pahath-moab, Adin, Elam, and the rest — had already appeared in the earlier register of Ezra 2; some of each house went up then, more went up now, as God inclined their hearts. Some, he says, were called into the vineyard at the third hour and others not till the eleventh, yet even the latecomers were not rejected. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the chapter's whole compass in a sentence: the genealogy of the chief persons who went with Ezra, the gathering at Ahava, the discovery that no Levites were present and the embassy to Casiphia, the proclaimed fast, the careful charge of the treasure, and the safe arrival at Jerusalem. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the register before us as the honour-roll of those who, when they might have stayed, chose the road home.
2:
The list proper begins with the priests and the one prince of David's house: “of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom; of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel; of the sons of David, Hattush.” The reformed John Gill fixes at once the caution the reader most needs, that this Daniel is not the famous prophet, who was of the royal blood and of the tribe of Judah, but a priest, a descendant of Ithamar, as Gershom was a descendant of Eleazar in the line of Phinehas. The two names, he shows, stand for two priestly lines reaching back to the sons of Aaron.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the genealogy with care. Gershom and Daniel are the names of heads of priestly houses, and “the sons of Phinehas” and “the sons of Ithamar” are designations of races: Phinehas was the son of the high priest Eleazar, the son of Aaron, and Ithamar a younger son of Aaron, as the pedigree of 1 Chronicles 6:3-4 records. This does not mean, they insist, that only these two priests went up with Ezra, for in Ezra 8:24 he will choose twelve from among the chief of the priests to have charge of the gifts; rather, Gershom and Daniel are the two heads of priestly houses who went, the one of the race of Phinehas and the other of the race of Ithamar. They note that a Daniel is named among the priests in Nehemiah 10:7, though whether he is the same man does not appear. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees in a word, marking Gershom as one of the descendants of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar.

Behind the bare names the witnesses feel the weight of the return. That the expedition should be headed by descendants of both the elder and the younger house of Aaron, and by a son of David through Hattush, is for them a quiet token that the whole covenant order — priesthood and monarchy alike — was being carried back to Jerusalem in seed. Keil and Delitzsch and Gill converge on the same double point: the register is exact, distinguishing this priestly Daniel from the prophet lest the reader confuse them, and it is representative, setting at the head of the migration the very lines through which God had promised to keep his sanctuary and his throne. The names are few, but they are chosen; the heads of Phinehas and Ithamar and the one shoot of David stand for the two great institutions that the second temple would need, and that this return was gathering home.
3:
With the third verse the register turns from priests and prince to the lay houses of the people: “of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty.” The reformed John Gill is careful to distinguish this Shechaniah from another of the same name who appears later in the book, for the register carries more than one bearer of it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same point: there were three men called Shechaniah, one here, a second at Ezra 8:6, and a third at Ezra 10:2, all different persons, as may be seen from their fathers' houses.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch survey the whole roll of lay houses at a stroke. Twelve are named both here and in the parallel list of First Esdras, and in ten of them the names of the races — Parosh, Pahath-moab, Adin, Elam, Shephatiah, Joab, Bebai, Azgad, Adonikam, and Bigvai — are identical in both texts, so that these ten families run back to the very houses that had returned with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:3 and following. Yet the form of this first house is peculiar, for before the name Zechariah stand two designations, “of the sons of Shechaniah” and “of the sons of Parosh,” where every other house has but one; and by comparison with the Greek they judge that Shechaniah is here not the head of the house but the wider clan, so that Zechariah of the sons of Parosh, of the family of Shechaniah, is the man who went up with a hundred and fifty males.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out a tender inference from the counting of “the males” only. Though the males alone are expressed, he observes, doubtless they carried the women along with them, as they did the little ones; the register numbers the men because on them the reckoning of a house depended, but it does not leave the wives and children behind. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke keep the several Shechaniahs distinct, Keil and Delitzsch fit the house of Parosh into the larger frame of the twelve families and their parallel in Zerubbabel's return, and Wesley reminds us that behind each round number of males stood whole households on the road. Together they read the verse as the first entry of the lay muster, a family that had sent some of its sons home under Zerubbabel and now sent more under Ezra, the covenant people returning by houses to the land of their fathers.
4:
The muster of the lay houses continues: “of the sons of Pahath-moab, Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males.” The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, taking the register in a single sweep, read this as the second of the twelve families whose names stand alike in the Hebrew and in the Greek of First Esdras, the house of Pahath-moab — literally “governor of Moab” — that had also sent home a great company under Zerubbabel, as the parallel roll of Ezra 2:6 records. Here its head is Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, who brought up two hundred of the males of his clan.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott's rule for the whole list governs this verse too: the name of the head of the house is followed by the wider family to which he belonged, so that Elihoenai is set down as one of the sons of Pahath-moab, a fresh contingent of an old and honoured house. And the number two hundred is not idle. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying the volunteers, had marvelled that the heads of the several families are named here for their honour, and the numbers of the males each brought in set down with them, amounting in all to 1496; the register is careful of these tallies because each represents so many souls willing to leave Babylon for Jerusalem when so many of their brethren would not stir.

The witnesses find in the very repetition of the house of Pahath-moab a lesson in the two returns. That the same families should appear in Ezra's list as in Zerubbabel's is, for Keil and Delitzsch, the mark of a people returning by stages: some of a house went up in the first migration under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and now, sixty and more years later, another portion of the same house went up under Ezra, so that the clans of the exile were gathered home not all at once but in successive companies as God inclined their hearts. Henry's reflection presides over the reading, that some were called into the vineyard at the third hour and others not till the eleventh, yet the latecomers were not rejected. The two hundred sons of Pahath-moab who followed Elihoenai are, in the witnesses' eyes, precisely such latecomers — an old house making a second answer to the call, adding its willing hundreds to the swelling roll of those who chose the road home. The register keeps their number as an honour, that a family's second devotion should not be forgotten.
5:
The list runs on to “the sons of Shechaniah, the son of Jahaziel, and with him three hundred males,” and here the witnesses pause over a gap in the text. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states it plainly: a name is obviously omitted, for the phrase “the son of Jahaziel” has lost the personal name of the head of the house that should have preceded it. The Greek of the Septuagint preserves what the Hebrew has dropped, reading “of the sons of Zattu, Shechaniah,” before Jahaziel — so that the family is that of Zattu, one of the houses that had returned with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:8, and its head Shechaniah the son of Jahaziel.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch had noted the same difficulty in surveying the whole roll: after “the sons of Shechaniah” there follows in the Hebrew only “Ben Jahaziel,” the son of Jahaziel, without the name of a head of house, exactly as at the tenth verse another name has fallen away. A comparison with the Septuagint and First Esdras, they judge, shows that it is not the personal name of the head that stands first in these entries but the name of the race, and that the copying has here lost a word. The two grammatical-historical witnesses thus agree in substance: the house is Zattu, its representative Shechaniah, and the Hebrew as it stands is defective, to be mended from the older Greek.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, counting the bearers of the name, reminds the reader that this Shechaniah is the second of three men so called in these chapters, distinct from the Shechaniah whose clan was named at the third verse and from the Shechaniah of the tenth chapter; the fathers' houses keep them apart, so that the same name deceives no careful reader. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch restore the missing house of Zattu from the Greek and treat the loss soberly as an ordinary accident of transcription, no wound to the substance of the record; Clarke keeps the several Shechaniahs distinct lest the names be confused.

Behind the textual repair the fact stands firm: three hundred more of the sons of the captivity, of an old returning house, cast in their lot with Ezra. The house of Zattu, like the houses of Parosh and Pahath-moab and Elam beside it, had already answered the call once under Zerubbabel; now it answers again, and the register, even where a copyist's slip has blurred a name, still bears witness to its number and its coming. What the witnesses honour is the readiness of a family to send its sons a second time, three hundred of them, to a city many of their kindred would not seek; and what they teach is that the flaw of a lost word neither hides that readiness nor diminishes the count, for the Greek preserves what the Hebrew dropped, and the willing three hundred keep their place in the roll of the second return.
7:
The roll comes to “the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him seventy males,” and the witnesses read it within the larger frame of the twelve lay houses. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reckon Elam among the ten families whose names stand identical in the Hebrew and in the Greek of First Esdras, an ancient and well-known house of the exile; for the sons of Elam had already sent a great company home under Zerubbabel, twelve hundred fifty and four of them, as the parallel register of Ezra 2:7 records. Now a further seventy of the house went up under Ezra, at their head Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott's principle for the whole list holds here: the name of the head, Jeshaiah, is joined to the wider family, the sons of Elam, to which he belonged, and the seventy males are reckoned by genealogy after the manner of the register. The comparison Ellicott draws throughout, between this later migration and the earlier one under Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:2 and following, gives the verse its meaning: the house of Elam appears in both, a family returning by portions, some of its sons in the first company and more in the second.

The witnesses find in so small an entry the same lesson the whole chapter teaches. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, meditating on the volunteers, had wondered that any could read the summons of the prophets and yet stay behind, and had honoured those who offered themselves willingly, their numbers set down family by family for a memorial. Seventy men of Elam, following Jeshaiah out of Babylon, are such willing volunteers; the number is modest beside the twelve hundred that went before, yet the register keeps it, for God inclined their hearts to go when their ease might have kept them. Some of a house, Henry observes, were called at the third hour and some not till the eleventh, and the eleventh-hour companies were not rejected. So the sons of Elam who came late are numbered here with honour beside those who came early, and the seventy who cast in their lot with Ezra stand in the sacred record as men who, when the door to Jerusalem stood open a second time, chose to walk through it. The register asks nothing more of them than that they came, and it does not let their coming be forgotten.
10:
Again the Hebrew shows a gap: “of the sons of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah, and with him an hundred and threescore males.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks it at once, that here also a name is wanting, for “the son of Josiphiah” has lost the personal name that should stand before it. The Septuagint, he shows, supplies the loss, reading “of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah” — so that the family is Bani, one of the houses of the first return named in Ezra 2:10, and its head Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, who brought up a hundred and sixty of the males of his clan.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch had set this beside the like defect at the fifth verse, where after “the sons of Shechaniah” only “Ben Jahaziel” followed, and here after “the sons of Shelomith” only “Ben Josiphiah,” in each case the name of the head of the house apparently dropped in the copying. Their conjecture, they say, is corroborated by the Greek of the Septuagint and First Esdras, which show that it is the name of the race, not the personal name of the head, that opens these entries, and that a word has here fallen away. The two grammatical-historical witnesses thus read the verse identically: the house is Bani, its representative Shelomith, and the Hebrew is to be completed from the older Greek.

The witnesses treat the loss with the same sobriety they show throughout the register. Such a slip of the pen, dropping a single name from a long list of families, is no ground for stumbling but the ordinary mark of a hand-copied text, and the older versions stand ready to mend it. What the mending recovers is another willing house: a hundred and sixty men of the sons of Bani, joining themselves to Ezra's company under Shelomith the son of Josiphiah. The number is preserved though the name was blurred, and the fact it records is sure — that yet another of the old returning houses of Ezra 2 put forth a fresh contingent for the second migration.

The parallel with the fifth verse is exact, and the witnesses feel its force. There the house of Zattu had lost its head's name and been restored from the Greek; here the house of Bani, in the very same way, has lost its Shelomith and is likewise restored. Twice within a few verses the Hebrew has dropped a name that the Septuagint and First Esdras retain, and twice the correction yields the same result — an old and honoured family sending a fresh company home under Ezra. The register, faithful even where a copyist faltered, keeps the count of those who came, so that the family of Bani should have its place among the households that chose Jerusalem over Babylon; and the reader learns, from these paired slips and their paired repairs, both how such lists were marred in the copying and how surely the substance of them may be recovered from the witnesses that stand alongside.
13:
The lay houses close with a phrase that catches the witnesses' eye: “of the last sons of Adonikam, whose names are these, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them threescore males.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads “the last sons” as the younger branches of the house, the elder having already been reported in the earlier return, among the six hundred sixty and six sons of Adonikam of Ezra 2:13. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the sense of the word, noting that the addition “last” marks these as the later or younger members of the family, the same usage found in the account of the men of Judah being “last” to bring back the king in 2 Samuel 19:11-12.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gives the reason the register troubles to note it: it seems the rest of the house of Adonikam came before, in the first migration, so that now, with these three heads and their sixty males, all the sons of that family had at length returned. None of Adonikam was any longer left in Babylon. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the same phrase and reports a division among interpreters over its drift. Some, he says, understand “the last sons of Adonikam” to their dispraise, as though they were the last and most reluctant to enlist themselves under Ezra, hanging back till the company was almost formed. Henry himself reads it rather to their honour: he takes it to mean that now all the sons of that family had returned and none stayed behind, the whole house at last gathered home.

So a small and genuine difference runs beneath the verse — whether “last” brands these sons as laggards or crowns the family for completing its return — yet the witnesses do not finally divide, for Henry's honourable reading and Wesley's plain statement agree that the point of the notice is the wholeness of the homecoming. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch fix the grammar, that these are the younger branches following the elder; Wesley and Henry fix the meaning, that with their coming the house of Adonikam was made complete. The register, having numbered house after house, ends its lay muster on a family that left none of its sons in exile, sixty men under three named heads closing the roll — a fitting seal on a list whose whole burden is the gathering of the scattered people, tribe by tribe and house by house, back to the land of promise.
14:
The lay register ends with the house of Bigvai: “of the sons also of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud, and with them seventy males.” The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that of Bigvai two heads are named, Uthai and Zabbud, who between them brought up seventy of the males of the clan; the same house had returned in force under Zerubbabel, as the parallel roll of Ezra 2:14 shows. They mark in passing how the Greek of First Esdras has corrupted these two plain names into an unrecognizable form, a warning of how easily such lists are marred in transmission, and how far the Hebrew is here to be preferred.

Keil and Delitzsch then cast up the whole account. The total number of individuals belonging to these twelve lay houses who returned with Ezra amounts, according to the Hebrew text, to 1496 males together with the fifteen heads of houses named at their head; according to First Esdras the sum is 1690 males and thirteen heads, and in neither reckoning are the priests and the sons of David counted, whose numbers are not stated. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the same Hebrew total, that the numbers of the males each family brought in amounted in all to 1496, and reads the sum as a modest but real answer to Ezra's call — a company small beside the multitude that stayed in Babylon, yet honoured man by man in the sacred record.

The witnesses close the muster with a backward glance over its whole design. That the historian should count the males of each house and then strike the grand total is, for Keil and Delitzsch, part of the exactness that runs through the register from the priests of the second verse to the sons of Bigvai here; the list is no vague reminiscence but a reckoning, family by family, of who came up. And the two differing totals, the Hebrew fifteen hundred and the Greek sixteen hundred and ninety, they weigh soberly as a variant of the versions rather than a flaw in the record. Henry's reflection gives the numbers their soul: these fifteen hundred were the willing remnant who, when they might have stayed at ease, shook themselves from the dust and followed Ezra home, and their tally stands for their honour. With the seventy sons of Bigvai the roll of the laity is complete, and the narrative is ready to turn from the naming of the houses to the gathering of them all at the river of Ahava.
15:
The register done, the narrative begins: “I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days: and I viewed the people, and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi.” The reformed John Gill locates the river, which gave its name to the place, and connects it with Adiabene, a district of Assyria named from the river Adiava. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reasons the same way, taking Ahava to be a river, perhaps the Diava or Adiava in the province of Adiabene, and perhaps the very region from which the men of Ava had been carried to Palestine by the king of Assyria in 2 Kings 17:24. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes Ahava for both river and town, reckons the journey thither at nine days from Babylon, and points to a place now called Hit, some eighty miles off, that has been identified with it.

The crisis of the verse is the missing Levites, and here the witnesses gather. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch narrate the moment: when the returning Israelites had assembled and were ready to start, Ezra reviewed them and perceived that there were no Levites among them, whereupon he took the measures the following verses record. Clarke and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sharpen the point that priests were present but Levites were not — none, that is, who were simply Levites and not of the priestly line. Ellicott adds the melancholy history behind the lack: only seventy-four Levites had returned with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:40, and here is fresh evidence that their disinclination to the temple service continued, so that Ezra's anxiety to supply the want is fully explained by the importance of Levitical ministry.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the absence into a rebuke and a wonder. Ezra took a view of his company at the appointed rendezvous and found there none of the sons of Levi, and Henry cries out at it: where was the spirit of that sacred tribe? Ezra, a priest, like Moses proclaims who is on the Lord's side, yet the Levites, unlike their father Levi of old, shrink back and desire to abide among the sheepfolds; they had their synagogues in Babylon and were loath to leave them, when they ought to have preferred the gates of Zion to all those meeting-places. It is upon record here to their reproach, Henry says, though he would rather it were not told in Gath. The witnesses do not divide. Gill, Clarke, and Ellicott fix the river and its place; Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, and Henry fix the alarming discovery and the reason it mattered, that a temple could not be served without the tribe ordained to serve it.
16:
Ezra acts at once upon the want, and the witnesses read the naming of his delegates as the work of a careful leader. “Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding.” The reformed John Gill observes that these were all in the camp, in some part of it, and Ezra sent messengers to summon them: three of them bore the same name, Elnathan; the first nine were men of chief note, rank, and dignity in their families, and the last two were noted as men of good sense, fit to plead a cause and so fit to be sent on such an errand.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the action forward to its purpose. Ezra sent these men with a charge to Iddo, the chief at the place Casiphia, and told them what they should say to Iddo and to his brethren the Nethinim, that they should bring to the company ministers for the house of God; and by the gracious help of God the delegates succeeded, inducing forty Levites and two hundred and twenty Nethinim, through Iddo's influence, to join their countrymen for the journey to Jerusalem. The mission named here, in other words, is the remedy for the lack just discovered, and its issue is already in view.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the two grades of men Ezra chose. The nine “chief men” were the heads and dignitaries of the company; the two “men of understanding,” he suggests, were teachers, and perhaps priests, joined with the nine chief men to form the deputation to Iddo. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the character of the envoys, nine notables and two men of sense, with the three Elnathans distinguished only by their office; Keil and Delitzsch fix the commission and its happy result; Ellicott fixes the two ranks and their likely calling. Together they show Ezra meeting the emergency not with complaint but with policy: he does not lament the missing Levites, he sends for them, choosing for the embassy men weighty enough to carry authority and wise enough to persuade, so that the house of God should not want its ministers. The verse is a small study in how a good work is furthered — by naming the right men and putting into their mouths the right words.
17:
The destination of the embassy draws the witnesses into a genuine dispute over geography. “And I sent them with commandment unto Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia.” The reformed John Gill, following Jarchi, takes Casiphia for a place in Babylon itself, a village near it or a quarter within it, where many of the Levites and Nethinim dwelt and where Iddo was chief over them; he expressly rejects the notion that it lay by the Caspian sea and mountains, as being too far off for the messengers to go and return in the time they had. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reasons the same way, setting Casiphia near Ahava, a colony of Jews presided over by Iddo — himself one of the humble race of the Nethinim, yet now their chief under the Persians — whose existence in those parts Ezra already knew.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the other road. The most judicious commentators, he holds, understand by Casiphia the Caspian mountains, between Media and Hyrcania, where the Nethinim were probably employed in working the silver mines; and he grounds the identification on the name, for the Hebrew keseph, from which Casiphia is drawn, signifies silver. So the debate is drawn: was Casiphia a Jewish settlement in or near Babylon, within easy reach of the camp at Ahava, or a distant mining district by the Caspian named from its silver? Gill and Ellicott hold the near place; Clarke holds the far.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hovers between the sense of the name and the sense of the errand. He too hears the silver in Casiphia — a Silver Street, one may call it, since ceseph signifies silver — and he pictures Iddo as the president of a college of Levites there, to whom Ezra sent not to urge the old man to come himself but to send some of the juniors, ministers for the house of God. On the purpose all the witnesses agree, whatever they make of the place. Ellicott glosses the “ministers” Ezra sought for as a term including both Levites and Nethinim, and Henry calls the furnishing of God's house with good ministers a good work that will redound to the comfort and credit of all who have a hand in it. The one difference is the map; the one accord is the aim — that from Casiphia, wherever it lay, Ezra meant to fetch the servants his sanctuary could not do without.
18:
The embassy prospers, and the witnesses ascribe its success where the text does: “by the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a man of understanding, of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel; and Sherebiah, with his sons and his brethren, eighteen.” The reformed John Gill dwells on that good hand, which favoured their designs, protected the messengers, and inclined those they were sent to — both the elders who had authority and the men themselves — to consent to what was proposed. The whole issue, he stresses, is laid not to Ezra's persuasion but to the providence of God working through it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on a nicety of the Hebrew. “A man of understanding” is probably not a description but a proper name, Ishsekel; this, he argues, is required by the conjunction “and” before Sherebiah, which would be out of place if the man of understanding and Sherebiah were the same person. Sherebiah himself was a Levite, the very man afterwards named by Nehemiah among those who expounded the law in Nehemiah 8:7. So the verse records at least two arrivals, a man named for his wisdom of the ancient stock of Mahli, and the Levite Sherebiah with eighteen of his sons and brethren.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the abiding lesson out of the opening phrase. If, where ministers have been wanting, the vacancies are well supplied, let us ascribe it to the good hand of God — qualifying them for the service, inclining them to it, and opening a door for them. The witnesses do not divide; their small difference over whether “a man of understanding” is a title or the name Ishsekel does not touch the substance, which is the recovery of the missing Levites through no strength of Ezra's own. Gill and Wesley read the good hand of God as the true agent of the whole affair, turning the hearts of a reluctant tribe; Ellicott fixes the persons who came, the descendant of Mahli and Sherebiah with his company. Together they make the verse a monument to answered prayer and providential grace: the tribe that had shrunk from the journey is at last represented, and the credit is given, before anything else is said, to the hand of God upon his people. The house that lacked its ministers begins, by that hand, to be furnished.
19:
The tale of the Levites recovered goes on: “and Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty.” The reformed John Gill notes that these were of the same division of the Levites as Sherebiah before them, so that the company gathered at Casiphia drew from more than one Levitical house. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place them precisely: Hashabiah and Jeshaiah were of the sons of Merari, one of the three great branches of Levi, and with their brethren and their sons they numbered twenty souls added to Ezra's train.

Keil and Delitzsch then look ahead to the humbler order that came with them, the Nethinim, whom David and the princes of Israel had given for the service of the Levites — made servants of the temple to perform its lowest offices. This appointment they connect with the ancient devoting of the Gibeonites to the sanctuary in Joshua 9:21 and with the return of the Nethinim under Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:43. That these too, like the notable men before them, should be “expressed by name” marks them as men of note, they add, comparing the mustered warriors distinguished by name in 1 Chronicles 12:31; the sacred record honours even the lowest servants of the house with a place in its roll.

The witnesses read the verse as the completing of a company. Where Sherebiah of the sons of Mahli had come first, now Hashabiah and Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari follow, so that more than one branch of Levi is represented and the tribe that had been wholly absent from the camp is present in fair number. Gill's small note, that these were of the same division as Sherebiah, and Keil and Delitzsch's careful placing of them among the Merarites, together show the historian's exactness: he does not merely say that Levites were found, but tells of what houses and in what numbers, twenty here after the eighteen before.

Keil and Delitzsch's forward glance to the Nethinim prepares the reader for the next verse, where the servants of the servants of the house are counted in their turn. The barren muster of the fifteenth verse, which found no son of Levi at all, is being filled, name by name and house by house, until the ministers of the sanctuary are supplied. And the witnesses do not miss the wonder that lies under the arithmetic: a tribe that had shrunk from the journey, whose absence had brought Ezra to a stand, is now yielding its men in twos and eighteens and twenties, drawn out of Casiphia by the embassy and the good hand of God. The eighteen of Mahli and the twenty of Merari are not many, but they are enough to begin the filling of the vacancy; and the record that had lamented an empty muster now grows, house by named house, into a company fit to serve the temple to which it is bound.
20:
The lowest order of the temple's servants is numbered last and honoured most particularly: “also of the Nethinim, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinim: all of them were expressed by name.” The reformed John Gill explains their office — they waited upon the Levites and ministered to them as the Levites ministered to the priests — and weighs their origin. Some think them the same as the Gibeonites whom Joshua devoted to the service of the sanctuary and David confirmed; others hold that these were a different body, an addition to the Gibeonites; Gill leaves the question open, content that they were the temple's bondservants set apart for its humblest work.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks a point of interest in the record itself: it is here alone that David is said to have appointed the Nethinim to aid the Levites, a notice preserved nowhere else. And he reads the closing clause with care. “All of them were expressed by name” means not, as some think, that they were all famous men, but that Iddo sent up their names in a list, a register of the two hundred and twenty which the historian does not here transcribe. The relief of their coming, Ellicott adds, is gratefully ascribed, like the coming of the Levites, to the good hand of God upon the company.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, who had traced the same servants to the ancient devoting of the Gibeonites and to their return under Zerubbabel, read the phrase “expressed by name” as marking them men of note, worthy of the honour of a place in the record. The witnesses do not sharply divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch weigh the Nethinim's descent from Joshua's Gibeonites or from a later gift; Ellicott fixes the singular notice of David's appointing them and the sense of the name-list Iddo forwarded. What all three feel is the fitness of the tally. Where the Levites themselves had held back, the Nethinim came in greater number, two hundred and twenty against the forty of Levi, more forward to serve than the tribe they were to serve under; and the historian, far from despising these lowly servitors, sets down that every one of them was named. The furnishing of the house is now complete: priests, Levites, and Nethinim, from the highest office to the lowest, are gathered for the journey, and the good hand of God is owned in the whole supply.
21:
With the company complete, Ezra turns from men to God: “Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance.” The reformed John Gill sets the fast in its moment, after the messengers to Iddo had returned with those they brought. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it as the last preparation for the march: the company being now complete, Ezra proclaimed a fast to humble themselves before God and to seek of him a prosperous journey for themselves, their families, and their goods. Fasting as a means of self-humbling, to obtain an answer to prayer, they show to be an ancient custom in Israel, citing Judges 20:26, 1 Samuel 7:6, Joel 1:14, and 2 Chronicles 20:3; and they gloss the “right way” as a straight and level road, cleared of obstruction, that is, a prosperous journey, in the sense of Psalms 112:7, while the “little ones” denote the whole household and the “substance” the goods and cattle of the travellers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the fast a school of prayer. Ezra had procured Levites, he says, but what will that avail unless he have God with him? That is his chief care. For public mercies public prayers must be made, that all who share the comfort may share the request; and their errand to the throne of grace was to seek the right way, to commit themselves to the guidance of divine providence and to beg that God would keep them and bring them safely to their journey's end. They were strangers in the road, Henry notes, bound to march through their enemies' country, and had no pillar of cloud and fire to lead them as their fathers had; but they believed the favour of God and the ministration of his angels would be to them instead of that. All our concerns, he adds, we ought by prayer to commit to God, after the counsel of Philippians 4:6.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fill out the fast's two ends. Ellicott points to the danger that made the seeking needful: the wilderness lay before them and an enemy in the way, the desert tribes that lie in wait for unprotected caravans; the “little ones” he takes as a sign that whole households went up, and the “substance” chiefly the treasures for the temple, with an undertone of abundance. Wesley reads the fast as kept for public mercies and for humiliation, that they might afflict themselves for their sins and so be qualified for pardon, seeking a safe and prosperous journey. The witnesses do not divide; together they show a leader who, having gathered his men and his treasure, will not stir a step until he has humbled his whole company before God and sought from him the road home.
22:
Ezra explains why he sought God rather than the king: “for I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way: because we had spoken unto the king, saying, The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him; but his power and his wrath is against all them that forsake him.” The reformed John Gill notes that Ezra might have had such a guard for the asking, so great was his interest in the king's favour; his shame, then, was not for want of means but for the sake of his testimony. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the confession the shame arose from: they had told the king that the hand of God is over all who seek him for good, and his power and wrath against all who forsake him — God's might, they explain, evidencing itself in wrath against the wicked and in strength to conquer all the enemies of his own.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the delicacy of Ezra's position. He had represented God, the object of his worship, as supremely powerful and as bearing the strongest affection for his true followers; he could not therefore, without contradicting himself, ask a band of soldiers to protect a company going expressly to rebuild God's worship. Were he to do so, the heathen might reckon his religion false and vain. So he found it necessary to seek the Lord by fasting and prayer, that they might have from God the succour without which they would fall a prey to their enemies; and thus, Clarke observes, this good man showed more anxiety for the glory of God than for his own personal safety.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the whole verse as looking back to the past: Ezra had magnified God's providence before the king, his “hand” upon his own for good — the habitual tribute to providence in this book and in Nehemiah — and his power against his enemies for evil. This sublime testimony had made the very seeking of God the condition of safety, and hence, Ellicott says, the solemn fasting and prayer that followed, after the precedents of Judges 20:26 and 1 Samuel 7:6. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds that Ezra was ashamed to ask a convoy lest he give the king and his court occasion to suspect either God's power to keep his people or Ezra's confidence in it; those who trust in God, he says, will be ashamed to seek to the creature for the protection they profess to have from him. The witnesses do not divide: the shame was the shadow of the confession, and the confession bound Ezra to trust the God he had so boldly preached.
23:
The fast issues in a granted prayer: “So we fasted and besought our God for this: and he was entreated of us.” The reformed John Gill reads it simply, that they sought the Lord by fasting and prayer for a good journey and preservation in it, and were heard. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses “he was entreated of us” as meaning that God gave them an assurance of his gracious answer to their request — a comfortable persuasion, before ever they set out, that their prayer had prevailed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his meditation on the fast, dwells on that success. They besought God by joint and public prayer, he says, and he was entreated of them; they had some comfortable assurance in their own minds that their prayers were answered, and the event afterward declared it, for never did any who sought God in earnest seek him in vain. In times of difficulty and danger, Henry urges, to set a season apart for prayer, whether secret or social, is the best method of relief we can take; and this company found it so, going out with a quiet confidence that the God to whom they had committed their way would keep it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch pass from the answered prayer to the next act it made possible, the safeguarding of the treasure. Ezra now separated twelve of the chief of the priests to take charge of the offerings; and here they pause over a difficulty of the text, that the words seem to read “to Sherebiah, Hashabiah,” as though these were among the twelve priests. But Sherebiah and Hashabiah, they observe, were not priests nor chiefs of priests at all, but Levites of the race of Merari, named in the eighteenth and nineteenth verses; to reckon them among the chiefs of the priests, or to make the priests their servants, would contradict the whole order of the ministry, so that the phrase must be otherwise construed. The witnesses do not divide. Gill, Wesley, and Henry rejoice in the plain mercy of the verse — a prayer heard, an assurance given, an errand never in vain; Keil and Delitzsch, reading on, mark the careful step that answered prayer next required, the committing of the sacred treasure to holy and reliable hands. The fast at Ahava thus bears its first fruit, a company sure of God's favour and free to turn to the ordering of the journey.
24:
Answered prayer does not excuse Ezra from prudence, and the witnesses watch him take order for the treasure: “then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them.” The reformed John Gill infers from the number that there were more priests in the company than the two named at the head of the register, very probably their families or brethren with them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott resolves the knotty grammar the previous witnesses had raised: the phrase is rather “to Sherebiah and Hashabiah,” meaning that these two Levites, alone mentioned by name, were with ten of their brethren associated with an equal number of priests in the charge of the temple treasure. The keeping of the gifts, that is, was laid jointly upon twelve priests and twelve Levites.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the whole arrangement a lesson in the marriage of faith and diligence. Having committed the keeping of the treasure to God, Ezra committed it also to proper men whose business it was to watch it; for our prayers must always be seconded with our endeavours, and the care of holy things must not be so left with God that it is not also entrusted to faithful men, after the rule Paul lays down in 2 Timothy 2:2. Do we expect God by his providence to keep what belongs to us? Let us by his grace keep what belongs to him. And who so fit to take charge of holy things, Henry asks, as holy persons? Those that have the dignity of the priesthood must take along with them the trust and duty of it.

The witnesses agree that the choice of these keepers was neither careless nor merely practical but fitted to the sacredness of the charge. Ellicott's careful construing shows the burden shared evenly between priests and Levites, twelve and twelve; Gill's small inference shows that the priestly company was larger than the register's two heads had suggested; Henry's meditation gives the theology, that God's honour and interest should be our care, and that the men set to guard the offerings of the sanctuary were chosen for their holiness as much as their number. Together they present Ezra as a steward who, having prayed for the safety of the treasure, now appoints watchful and consecrated hands to bear it — twelve chief priests and their Levite brethren — so that the gifts devoted to the house of God should travel under a guard worthy of them. The verse opens the careful transaction of weighing and charging that the next verses will complete.
25:
The treasure is now delivered by exact weight: “and weighed unto them the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, even the offering of the house of our God, which the king, and his counsellors, and his lords, and all Israel there present, had offered.” The reformed John Gill reads the weighing as an act of prudence and integrity: Ezra did it as a proof of his own faithfulness, a security against any charge of embezzling, an example to the keepers, and a safeguard that they too should be free from temptation and vindicated against suspicion. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that to weigh is to deliver by weight, and that the offering was the gold and silver and vessels given for the house of God by the king, his counsellors and lords, and all the Israelites who were found in Babylon and were not themselves returning — the freewill gifts already described in Ezra 7:15-16.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the scale of the thing. The gold and silver, he notes, were in bars or ingots; and according to the best computation the silver would amount to something like a quarter of a million of our money, and the gold to about three-quarters of a million — a treasure of enormous value to be carried, unguarded by soldiers, across a wilderness full of robbers. The very greatness of the sum, in the witnesses' reading, throws into relief the boldness of the faith that would not ask the king for an escort.

The witnesses find in the deliberate weighing a moral as well as a method. Gill draws out the principle that in all trusts, and especially sacred ones, a man should be so open in his dealing that neither he nor those under him can be justly suspected; the weighing was a public reckoning that left everything clear. Keil and Delitzsch fix the source of the gifts, the piety of a Persian king and his court and of the Jews who stayed behind but would still enrich the temple they did not return to. Ellicott fixes the sheer weight of gold and silver that this faith committed to the road. Together they show Ezra handling the offerings of the house of God with a scrupulous exactness that matched the confidence of his prayer: he had trusted God to keep the treasure, and he now took every human care that its keeping should be honest and accountable, weighing out coin and vessel into the hands of the men he had set apart, that all might be forthcoming at the journey's end.
26:
The verse sets down the great sum in figures: “I even weighed unto their hand six hundred and fifty talents of silver, and silver vessels an hundred talents, and of gold an hundred talents.” The reformed John Gill reckons the value in the money of his own day, the six hundred and fifty talents of silver amounting, on one computation, to some two millions and more of pounds sterling, the hundred talents of silver vessels to tens of thousands; and he records the tradition of Jarchi and Aben Ezra that there were a hundred such vessels, each of a talent's weight. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply set the amounts in order — six hundred and fifty talents of silver, a hundred talents of silver vessels, a hundred talents of gold — and carry the reckoning on into the golden basins and the vessels of fine copper that the next verse will name.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke corrects a possible misreading and computes the whole. “Silver vessels a hundred talents” means the total weight of all the silver vessels amounted to a hundred talents, not that there were a hundred vessels each of a talent; and reckoning in round sums he casts the silver, the silver vessels, and the gold together into a sum above a million sterling, with the golden basins yet to be added. Clarke is candid that the different weights and coins are variously computed, some making the talent much less, so that the figures are estimates rather than certainties; but by any reckoning the treasure was vast.

Clarke then turns, as he loves to do, to a curiosity of metallurgy, the “two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold,” that stood among the offerings. The Syriac, he reports, took them for vessels of the best Corinthian brass, the famed alloy said to have been formed when gold, silver, and copper ran molten together at the burning of Corinth; but Clarke judges them rather some factitious metal, artfully compounded, that took a polish and a lustre like gold and resisted tarnish, more durable and for many uses more valuable than gold itself. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Gill and Clarke labour the sterling values and the disputed talents; Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain catalogue; all agree that a treasure of many hundred talents of silver and gold, with vessels of silver and of a strange bright copper, was weighed out into the keepers' hands — wealth enough to tempt an army, carried by faith across the desert.
27:
The catalogue of the treasure is completed: “also twenty basons of gold, of a thousand drams; and two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold.” The reformed John Gill computes the golden basins by the value of the coin: the twenty were of a thousand drams, and the Persian daric or drachm, he reports on the authority of Bishop Cumberland, weighed some twenty shillings and fourpence, so that the basins were worth upward of a thousand pounds of English money; Dr. Bernard, he adds, reckoned the daric to exceed one of our guineas by two grains. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the reckoning: the “thousand drams” are darics, and the twenty basins were therefore worth rather more than a thousand guineas.

Over the two vessels of fine copper the witnesses linger with the same wonder they showed at the previous verse. Ellicott identifies the metal, probably, with the Roman orichalcum, a substance very highly valued in antiquity, brighter and costlier than common brass. The phrase “precious as gold” is no loose praise but a measured judgment: two vessels of a copper so fine and so artfully wrought that they were rated with the gold and silver among the offerings of the house of God.

The witnesses read the small inventory as of a piece with the great one before it. Gill and Ellicott agree that even the least items of the treasure were reckoned to their exact worth, the basins by the weight of their darics and the copper vessels by their rarity, so that nothing devoted to the temple should pass without its precise account. The care that weighed the six hundred and fifty talents weighed also the twenty basins and the two bright vessels; the God to whom they were given was served with an exactness that despised nothing and slurred nothing.

The presence, among the gold and silver, of two vessels of a costly copper “precious as gold” speaks, to the witnesses' eye, of the varied liberality of the givers — kings and counsellors and common Israelites enriching the sanctuary out of what each held dearest, whether bullion or basin or a rare and shining alloy. That such vessels should be rated with the gold, and set down by name in the inventory, tells the witnesses how highly the ancient world prized this bright and durable metal, and how freely the friends of the temple bestowed even their choicest things upon it. The whole treasure now stands numbered and weighed, the great talents and the golden basins and the two vessels of fine copper alike, ready for the solemn charge Ezra is about to lay upon its keepers, that these holy things be kept holy until they reach Jerusalem. Nothing has been left unvalued; the offering of the house of God is complete, down to the last shining vessel, before it is committed to the road.
28:
Ezra now consecrates the keepers as well as the gift: “and I said unto them, Ye are holy unto the LORD, the vessels are holy also; and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering unto the LORD God of your fathers.” The reformed John Gill draws out the double holiness: as the men were dedicated and set apart to holy service, so the vessels were sacred to holy uses, and neither the one nor the other might be turned to any common purpose. The charge binds the sanctity of the persons to the sanctity of the things they bear.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls it a unique verse in every respect, and finds its force in that same joining: the treasures were consecrated, and they were committed to consecrated hands, so that a good account might be given of them to the treasurers of the temple. The fitness Ellicott hears in the words is the whole point — holy things entrusted to holy men, that holiness might guard holiness all the way to Jerusalem. Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the charge, reason to the same end: because the priests and Levites were themselves holy to the Lord, they were to treat and keep the gifts committed to them as holy gifts, until on their arrival they should weigh them out again before the priests and princes in the chambers of the house of the Lord.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the charge its deepest resonance. Ezra tells the keepers why he puts these things into their hands: you are holy unto the Lord, and the vessels are holy also, and who so fit to take care of holy things as holy persons? Those who have the dignity and honour of the priesthood must take along with them the trust and the duty of it. Henry hears behind Ezra's words the prophet's summons to the returning exiles in Isaiah 52:11, “be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD” — a purity of life required precisely of those who carry what is sacred. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the twofold holiness of men and vessels, Ellicott the unique fitness of consecrated gifts in consecrated hands, Keil and Delitzsch the obligation it laid on the keepers, Henry the abiding demand that the bearers of holy things be themselves holy. Together they make the verse a charter of sacred stewardship: the treasure is the Lord's freewill gift, the keepers are the Lord's set-apart servants, and the one is safe in the other's keeping only so long as both remain what they are called — holy unto the Lord.
29:
The charge is pressed home with the word “watch”: “watch ye, and keep them, until ye weigh them before the chief of the priests and the Levites, and chief of the fathers of Israel, at Jerusalem, in the chambers of the house of the LORD.” The reformed John Gill glosses the command plainly — the vessels, the silver, and the gold were to be so watched and kept that they should not be hurt nor diminished on the way. The vigilance required was to guard the treasure entire until it could be handed over. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the terms of the trust: the keepers were to watch and keep the gifts until they weighed them out before the chief priests, the Levites, and the heads of the fathers' houses of Israel, in the chambers of the temple; and they carry the account forward, that the priests and Levites accordingly received the treasure by weight to bring it to Jerusalem, and that the company then set out from Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expands the single word “watch” into the whole discipline of a sacred trust. “Watch ye, and keep them,” Ezra says, that they be not lost, nor embezzled, nor mingled with the other articles; keep them together, keep them by themselves, keep them safely, until you weigh them in the temple before the great men there. The very form of the charge, Henry notes, intimates how much it was the keepers' concern to be careful and faithful, and how much their honour to be found so. And he hears in it the echo of Paul's charge to Timothy: as the apostle, committing the gospel treasure, bade him keep it until the appearing of Jesus Christ, so Ezra bids his keepers hold the sacred vessels safe until the day of reckoning at Jerusalem, when fidelity would be their crown, after the manner of the trust urged in 2 Timothy 1:14.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain aim, that nothing be damaged or lost; Keil and Delitzsch fix the appointed terminus, a public weighing before the assembled dignitaries in the temple chambers; Henry fixes the moral weight, that a trust received by weight must be discharged by weight, and that those who keep holy things must one day give a particular account of them. Together they show the charge closing the transaction of the treasure: it was weighed into the keepers' hands, and it must be weighed out of them, so that the same exactness which delivered it should also receive it, and the faithfulness of the bearers stand proved before the whole assembly at the journey's end.
30:
The keepers accept the charge: “so took the priests and the Levites the weight of the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem unto the house of our God.” The reformed John Gill identifies them as the twelve priests and twelve Levites named before, into whose joint keeping the treasure was now committed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verb precisely: they “took the weight” of the silver and gold and vessels, that is, they received by weight what had been delivered to them by weight, so that the amount they carried away answered exactly to the amount weighed out. The transaction is deliberately symmetrical: what was given by tale and weight is received by tale and weight, and the keepers are bound to render it so again.

The witnesses feel the quiet solemnity of the receiving. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose meditation governs this whole passage, had insisted that our prayers must be seconded with our endeavours, and that the care of holy things, though committed to God, must also be committed to faithful men; here that committing is completed. The priests and Levites take up the burden “to bring them to Jerusalem unto the house of our God” — the destination naming the purpose of the whole trust, for the treasure was not theirs but the Lord's, gathered for his house and now borne toward it by the men he had set apart.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brief verse repays its weight. Gill fixes who the bearers were, the four-and-twenty consecrated men; Keil and Delitzsch fix the manner of the taking, by exact weight, that the account might be closed without loss; Henry supplies the spirit, that a sacred trust is honourably borne when faithful hands take up what holy prayer has commended to God. The gifts of a Persian king and of the scattered people of God, weighed out at Ahava into these hands, now begin their journey to the temple.

There is, the witnesses feel, a quiet fitness in the very symmetry of the transaction. The treasure was delivered by weight and is received by weight; it was committed to men set apart as holy and is borne by those same holy hands; it was prayed over before it was handled and is now carried under the shadow of that prayer. The keepers have received their charge and shouldered it, and the company stands ready to depart. What was devoted to the house of God is on its way to the house of God, guarded not by soldiers but by the holiness of its keepers and the good hand of the God whose it is. The register of families and the reckoning of talents have alike been closed; nothing remains but to set out, and the taking-up of the burden here is the last act before the road.
31:
The march begins at last: “then we departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go unto Jerusalem: and the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy, and of such as lay in wait by the way.” The reformed John Gill dates the setting-out to the month Nisan, two days before the passover began. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reconcile the day with the earlier notice that the journey from Babylon was appointed for the first of the month in Ezra 7:9: on the first day the company began to gather, and during the three days' encampment at Ahava Ezra discovered that no Levites were present, took the measures to fetch them, and proclaimed the fast, so that it was the twelfth before the whole company could actually move.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry attends the travellers the whole way. His God was good, and Ezra acknowledged the goodness: the hand of God was upon them to animate them for the undertaking, to preserve them from the enemies that lay in wait by the way to do them a mischief or, like Amalek of old, to smite the hindmost. Even the common perils of a journey, Henry reflects, oblige us to sanctify our going out with prayer and our return in peace with thanksgiving; much more such a dangerous expedition as this, carrying a great treasure through hostile country without a guard. That they were brought safely on their road, and afterward safely to their journey's end, he lays wholly to the good hand of God that had begun the good work and would perform it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sums the matter in a phrase, that “the hand of our God was upon us” gathers up the whole history of the journey into a single confession of providence. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the date and its nearness to the passover; Keil and Delitzsch reconcile the twelfth day with the first by the delay over the Levites and the fast; Henry and Ellicott read the deliverance from the lurking enemy as the vindication of Ezra's bold faith, that the God whom he had refused to distrust by asking a royal escort did in fact bring his people through. The very peril the fast had been proclaimed against — the ambushes of the desert — is here named as the peril from which God delivered them, so that the answered prayer of the twenty-third verse and the safe passage of this one stand together as one testimony: those who seek God are kept under the shadow of his wings, even in their greatest dangers.
32:
The travellers arrive: “and we came to Jerusalem, and abode there three days.” The reformed John Gill reads the pause as a needful rest before any business was done — before they delivered what had been committed to them for the temple, or the commissions to the king's officers — for it was but proper they should have some repose after so fatiguing a journey. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees, taking the three days as devoted, like the similar interval in Nehemiah's case, to rest and to more private devotion after the long road.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the date and the duration of the whole march. They arrived, as Ezra 7:9 had stated, on the first day of the fifth month, the journey from Ahava having occupied some three months and a half; and after their arrival they remained, as Nehemiah afterward did in Nehemiah 2:11, quiet and inactive for three days, to recover from the hardships of the way before they undertook the ordering of their affairs. On the fourth day, they add, the treasure was delivered in the house of God into the hands of Meremoth and Eleazar the priests and two Levites, the chiefs of the priests and Levites being present, as the following verses will relate.

The witnesses read the three days' rest as itself a mark of wisdom and reverence. Gill and Ellicott hear in it both the ordinary prudence of men worn with travel and the piety of a company that would not rush from the road into the sacred business of the temple, but would first compose themselves in quiet and prayer. Keil and Delitzsch fix the exact chronology, the arrival on the first of the fifth month after three months and a half, and the deliberate quiet of the three days before the weighing of the gifts.

The parallel with Nehemiah, which both Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch draw, gives the pause its meaning. Nehemiah too, on reaching Jerusalem, remained three days before he stirred to his work; and the recurrence of the pattern suggests to the witnesses a settled propriety in it — that the servant of God, come to a great task, first rests and prays before he acts. Together they show the migration reaching its goal not in a tumult of haste but in ordered calm: the company that had set out with fasting and prayer arrives to rest and devotion, and only on the fourth day, refreshed and recollected, turns to render up the treasure it had borne so far. The long road from Ahava ends, fittingly, not at the treasury door but in three days' stillness; and out of that stillness the discharge of the trust, and the worship that crowns it, will presently begin. The journey is over; the sacred business is about to open.
33:
The trust is now discharged with the same exactness that received it: “now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest.” The reformed John Gill notes only the timing, the fourth day after their arrival, when the three days' rest was over. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name the officers who received the treasure: it was weighed into the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest, with Eleazar the son of Phinehas beside him, and with them Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites — two priests and two Levites, answering to the keepers who had borne it. Everything, they add, was reckoned by number and by weight, and the whole weight was written down at that time, an authentic record made at the very moment of delivery.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the men and lends them a history: these names of the priests and Levites who officially received the treasures occur again in Nehemiah, so that the officers of this weighing were known and traceable figures in the later record of the restored community. Meremoth the son of Uriah, in particular, reappears in Nehemiah's account of the building of the wall, a real and identifiable person whose hands took charge of the sacred gifts.

The witnesses read the weighing at Jerusalem as the deliberate counterpart of the weighing at Ahava. What Ezra had delivered to the keepers by number and weight, that they now render up by number and weight, before named and responsible officers, and the sum is set down in writing for a lasting witness. Gill fixes the day, Keil and Delitzsch the four officers and the careful record, Ellicott the reappearance of these same men in Nehemiah. Together they show the trust closed exactly as it was opened: no vessel lost, no talent unaccounted, the whole treasure passed from consecrated hand to consecrated hand and its full weight recorded in the house of God. The charge Ezra laid at Ahava — to watch and keep the gifts until they were weighed before the chief priests and Levites in the temple chambers — is here fulfilled to the letter, and the faithfulness of the bearers stands proved before the assembly, the sacred treasure safe home in the sanctuary for which it was given.
34:
The weighing is registered to the last particular: “by number and by weight of every one: and all the weight was written at that time.” The reformed John Gill draws out the double reckoning: the vessels and the treasure were delivered in by tale and by weight, and these exactly agreed with the number and the weight in which they had been received at Ahava. Nothing had been lost or altered on the way; the account balanced to the grain. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the purpose of so meticulous a record: the number of the vessels and the weight of the ingots were written down and laid up for security, an authentic register kept against any future question or claim.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the same clause, read “by number, by weight, as to all” to mean that all was delivered by number and weight, and that the whole weight was written at that time, that is, an authentic list was drawn up at the very delivery. The three witnesses converge on the single point: everything was counted, everything was weighed, and the totals were committed to writing on the spot.

The witnesses find in this small verse the seal of the whole careful transaction. From the first weighing at the river to the last at the temple, the treasure had been handled with a scrupulous exactness, and now that exactness is made permanent in a written record. Gill fixes the agreement of the two reckonings, the received and the delivered; Ellicott the safekeeping of the register; Keil and Delitzsch the drawing-up of the list at the moment of delivery.

Together they show why such pains were taken. Holy things demand honest handling, and honest handling demands a clear account; those who bear the offerings of the house of God must be able to show that they have borne them faithfully. The written weight was at once a vindication of the keepers, who could prove they had lost nothing, and a witness to the reverence with which the whole company treated what was devoted to God. Nor was the record for that day only: Ellicott's remark that it was laid up for security means it stood as a permanent muniment, a document to be appealed to if ever the account should be questioned. So the treasure passed into the temple not only intact but on record, every talent and every vessel numbered, weighed, and written, that the faithfulness of the stewardship might stand beyond dispute. The whole journey of the gifts, from the freewill hands that gave them to the temple chambers that received them, is thus closed with a written witness that nothing had been lost and nothing embezzled — the fitting end of a trust begun in prayer and borne by holy hands.
35:
The returned exiles turn from delivering the treasure to worshipping the God who brought them home: “also the children of those that had been carried away, which were come out of the captivity, offered burnt offerings unto the God of Israel, twelve bullocks for all Israel, ninety and six rams, seventy and seven lambs, twelve he goats for a sin offering.” The reformed John Gill identifies the worshippers as those who had now come up with Ezra, the children of the captivity. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the sacrifices as an act of gratitude for the gracious restoration of God's people: twelve bullocks for all Israel, that is, for the twelve tribes, and twelve he-goats for a sin offering, as at the earlier dedication in Ezra 6:17; the ninety-six rams they note as eight times twelve, and the seventy-seven lambs as the intensified seven. The sin offering, they observe, went before the burnt offering as its necessary basis, availing to atone for the sins of all Israel, that the surrender typified by the burnt offering might be accepted.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the meaning of the numbers. Adam Clarke marvels that though only the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were properly present, they offered a bullock for every tribe, as if all were there; and he judges there were doubtless individuals present from all the twelve tribes, some families of each, though no whole tribe but those two. John Wesley draws out the symbolism: they offered twelve bullocks, twelve he-goats, and ninety-six rams, eight times twelve, signifying the union of the two kingdoms; they no longer went, two tribes one way and ten another, but all the twelve met, by their representatives, at the same altar.

Wesley presses further the necessity of the sin offering, for it is the atonement that secures every mercy to us, which will not be truly comfortable unless iniquity be taken away and our peace made with God. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the worshippers, the children of the captivity newly come; Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke and Wesley together read the offerings as at once thanksgiving and atonement, and the recurring number twelve as the confession of a reunited Israel. What strikes them all is that a remnant chiefly of Judah and Benjamin should yet sacrifice for the whole twelve tribes, laying hold by faith on the ancient unity of the people of God even in the day of their fewness; and that before they rejoiced in a burnt offering wholly surrendered to God, they first confessed their sin over the he-goats, knowing that no mercy is sweet until sin is put away. So the journey ends where it should, at the altar, in penitence and praise.
36:
The last verse turns from the altar to the civil powers: “and they delivered the king's commissions unto the king's lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God.” The reformed John Gill identifies the officers as the governors of the provinces of Syria, Palestine, and Judea, which lay on that side of the Euphrates where the land of Israel was. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that the royal decrees — the very commission of Ezra 7:12-26 — were now delivered to the satraps of the king and to the governors beyond the river, who thereupon furthered the people and the house of God, as Artaxerxes had commanded them to do.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses over the title rendered “the king's lieutenants,” the Hebrew achashdarpeney, a word generally understood to mean lieutenant or deputy and probably of Persian origin, though here much corrupted; the Vulgate renders it “to the satraps of the king,” which is the Persian satrab, and Clarke traces the sense through the Persian terms for a viceroy and for a man of trust. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott distinguishes the two grades of officer: the king's commission, or firman, was delivered to the lieutenants or satraps in military authority, and to the governors, the pechahs or pashas, in civil authority under them; and the firman was of course accepted and acted upon, so that “they furthered the people.”

Ellicott marks the fine order of the chapter's close: first came the sacrifices of burnt offering to God, and then, having rendered to God the things that were God's, they render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, delivering the royal commission to the officers of the empire. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the officers and the decrees they received; Clarke unfolds the Persian title of the satraps; Ellicott distinguishes the military and civil authorities and hears in the sequence — sacrifice first, then the king's business — the right proportion of duty. And all agree on the happy issue named in the last clause: the officers of a heathen empire, bound by their master's writ, furthered both the people and the house of God. The chapter that began with a register of volunteers leaving Babylon ends with the powers of the world bowing to the king's commission and speeding the work of the temple, so that the returning exiles, having sought God with fasting and been kept by his hand through the wilderness, find even their former masters made helpers of their God.
